title: Stoned at Ta'if
hook: he walks to Ta'if to seek help, and is mocked and driven out

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Talib: the uncle who shielded him died, and the street could reach him. Your line was: the shield is gone.

Mecca has closed its doors. The wife who held him is buried. The uncle who shielded him is buried. So he does something that takes nerve: he leaves, on foot, for Ta'if, a town in the hills, to ask its tribe, Thaqif, for help and a hearing. No army, no escort of clan, no promise of welcome. He's going to knock on the doors of strangers and say what he has said in Mecca. Today: Ta'if.
screen: `MECCA HAS CLOSED.` → `ON FOOT TO THE HILLS.` → `KNOCKING ON STRANGERS' DOORS.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq says he went to the leaders of Thaqif, three brothers, sat with them and told them why he'd come. Their answers are sharp. One says, in effect, if God sent you, I'll tear the covering of the Ka'ba. Another: couldn't God find anyone but you to send? The third: I won't speak to you at all. If you're really a messenger, you're too great for me to answer, and if you're lying, you're not worth answering. Three doors, shut. He gets up and asks them one thing: then keep this between us. They don't. They stir up the people of the town, and, as the accounts tell it, a crowd follows him out, jeering and shouting, and in some tellings throwing stones, until he reaches an orchard outside town and takes shelter by its wall. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps his own words about a day like this. Years later, Aisha asks whether he ever had a day harder than the battle of Uhud. He says the worst was the day of al-Aqabah, when he offered himself to Ibn Abd Yalil and was turned away; commentators connect that day with Ta'if. He went off with his grief, he says, not knowing where he was going, and didn't come to himself until he reached a place called Qarn al-Tha'alib. The man Muslims honor as the final messenger tells his wife that he walked in a daze. The story doesn't hide it. But notice the verb. He went. Hurt and dazed, he kept walking. What he said and met along that road is the next few days.
screen: `THREE BROTHERS, THREE NOS.` · `KEEP THIS BETWEEN US.` · `A CROWD, AND STONES.` · `HE WALKED IN A DAZE.` · then, large: `HE KEPT WALKING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one no you've been given lately, a job, an apology not accepted, and let it be as heavy as it is. Then, if you can, take a few slow steps across the room, feeling each foot land, or, if you can't walk right now, press each foot into the floor in turn. You don't have to feel better to take the next step, and if you pray, you can bring that no to Allah as it is.
Ta'if. The hill town where he went for help, was turned away, mocked and driven out, and kept walking. Today's word.
Your line: he walked on. Not healed yet, just walking. Day seven hundred fifty, done.

howItsDone: Muslims learn the journey to Ta'if as part of the Meccan sirah, retold just before the night journey, and it is remembered when people face rejection.

chat.says: What happened when the Prophet went to Ta'if for help?
options: Its leaders refused him, a crowd drove him out, and he walked on.
Thaqif welcomed him, and Ta'if became the first Muslim town.
He fought the leaders of Ta'if and won the town over by force.
chat.meaning: Ibn Ishaq says the three brothers of Thaqif turned him away and stirred up the town. In Bukhari he says he walked on in grief.

Ta'if.meaning: a town in the hills, home of the Thaqif tribe

Qarn al-Tha'alib.meaning: the place where he came back to himself

Aisha.meaning: his wife, who asked him about his hardest day

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the journey to Ta'if; the three brothers of Thaqif and their replies; the request for secrecy; the crowd; the orchard)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3231 (Aisha asks of a day harder than Uhud; Ibn Abd Yalil; he walked in grief until Qarn al-Tha'alib)

notes: Index hook says 'mocked and stoned out'; Ibn Ishaq's text as recalled speaks of louts and slaves insulting him and crying after him; the stones come from other accounts. Script says 'as the accounts tell it'. Confirm.
The three brothers' replies are paraphrased from Ibn Ishaq as recalled; confirm.

Bukhari 3231 places this 'the day of Aqabah' with Ibn Abd Yalil ibn Abd Kulal; commentators link it to Ta'if. Confirm the link is fair, and that tomorrow's/day 753's use of the same hadith doesn't overlap too much.
'The man Muslims honor as the final messenger' is a description of Muslim belief, not a claim by the narrator; confirm it reads that way.
Hook description of Ta'if as 'a town in the hills' and the original note 'in the mountains near Mecca' are geographic generalities; confirm.
